en: The Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā.
Homage to the Buddha!
Then, at that time, the venerable Upāli rose from his seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Lord, here, while I was alone in seclusion with a mind withdrawn in meditation, this reflection arose in my mind:
'The Prātimokṣa restraint has been prescribed by the Blessed One as the training in higher ethics and its purification for those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
however, for those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, the Blessed One has taught and pointed out that even the training must be maintained here, even at the cost of one's life.'"
In that case, how should the Prātimokṣa restraint be described for those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, whether the Blessed One has entered parinirvāṇa or is still remaining?
How should it be described for those belonging to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle? And how should the Prātimokṣa restraint be described for Bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna?
"I have been designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who are devoted to the Vinaya.

Therefore, O Blessed One, please instruct me; may the Blessed One reveal skill in means, so that having heard it directly from the presence of the Blessed One and having received it directly, I may attain fearlessness and proclaim it in detail before the assemblies."
"Blessed One, as I was alone, in seclusion, and in retreat, this reflection arose in my mind: 'What if I were to approach the Blessed One and inquire about the determination of the Vinaya?
Therefore, Blessed One, may the Tathāgata please explain the determination of the Vinaya in detail, for a great assembly of monks and an assembly of bodhisattvas have gathered."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Upāli:
"Therefore, Upāli, speak of the purity of training for those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle with one application and one intention;
speak of the purity of training for those established in the Mahāyāna with another application and another intention."

For what reason? Because, Upāli, the application of those belonging to the vehicle of the disciples is one thing, and their resolute intention is another; the application of those who have set out in the Great Vehicle is another, and their resolute intention is another.

In this regard, Upāli, that which is pure ethical discipline for one belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas is impure ethical discipline and the ultimate transgression of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna.

That which is pure ethical discipline for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna is impure ethical discipline and the ultimate transgression of ethical discipline for one belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
For what reason?
"Upāli, here a follower of the Śrāvaka vehicle does not take up rebirth in existence even in a single momentary thought.
This is the purity of ethical discipline for one of the Śrāvaka vehicle; yet it is the impurity of ethical discipline and the ultimate immorality for a Bodhisattva of the Mahāyāna.

Upāli, what is the purity of ethical discipline for a Bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna, which constitutes the impurity of ethical discipline and the ultimate immorality for one of the Śrāvaka vehicle?"
"Upāli, here a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna accepts rebirth in existence for immeasurable and incalculable eons with an untiring heart and an untiring mind.

This is the purity of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna; whereas for one belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, that same [conduct] is impure ethical discipline and the height of immorality.
Therefore, Upāli, you should speak to those bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna regarding their training which must be guarded."
Speak of the training that requires no protection for those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle; speak of the training that involves exceptions for the Bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna;
speak of the training that is without exception for those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Speak of the training that has entered deeply for those bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna; speak of the training with its successive stages for those belonging to the Śrāvakayāna.

And how, Upāli, is the training of the bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna one characterized by protection, while the training of those belonging to the Śrāvakayāna is one without protection?

"Upāli, here a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna should follow after the welfare of other beings and other persons, whereas one belonging to the Śrāvakayāna does not. By this method, Upāli, the training of the bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna is accompanied by protection, while the training of those of the Śrāvakayāna is without protection.
And how, Upāli, is the training of the bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna accompanied by exemptions, whereas the training of those of the Śrāvakayāna is without exemptions?"
"Upāli, even if a bodhisattva who has set out in the Great Vehicle should incur an offense in the morning, if he should dwell at midday unseparated from the mind of omniscience, he remains limitless;
such is the aggregate of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna.
If he should incur an offense at midday, if he should dwell in the evening unseparated from the mind of omniscience, he remains limitless."
Such is the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) of a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna.
If he should commit an offense in the evening, yet should dwell during the first watch of the night without being separated from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatācitta*), it remains limitless.
Such is the aggregate of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna.
If one should incur an offense during the first watch of the night and should dwell without interruption during the middle watch of the night, never being separated from the mind of omniscience—
such is the aggregate of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna.

If one should incur an offense during the middle watch of the night and should dwell without interruption during the final watch of the night, never being separated from the mind of omniscience— [such is the aggregate of ethical discipline].
In this way, the aggregate of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna is to be understood.

For in this manner, Upāli, is the training with its exemptions for bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna. In that regard, a bodhisattva should not give rise to the obsession of remorse, nor should he be excessively full of regret.

In that regard, Upāli, if one belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayānika*) should repeatedly commit an offense, it should be understood that the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) of that follower of the disciple-vehicle has been destroyed.
For what reason?
Because one who belongs to the disciple-vehicle must act as if their head and clothing were on fire in order to abandon all afflictions (*kleśa*).

In this way, Upāli, the training of one belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle who desires parinirvāṇa is indeed without exception. But how, Upāli, is the training of those bodhisattvas set out in the Mahāyāna far-reaching? The training of those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle is with interruption. Here, Upāli, a bodhisattva set out in the Mahāyāna, even after sporting, delighting, and enjoying himself with the five strands of sensual pleasure for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, does not abandon the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
"Upāli, this should be understood as the training for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna.
For what reason?

Upāli, there will come a time, there will come an occasion, when a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna, by virtue of that very bodhicitta being well-sustained, will not be overcome by any afflictions even while in a dream."
It will be withdrawn.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna should not exhaust all afflictions in a single lifetime;
rather, the afflictions of bodhisattvas come to exhaustion gradually.

Moreover, Upāli, one who belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas and whose roots of virtue are fully ripened—like one whose hair and clothes are on fire—should not, even for a single moment, bring about rebirth in existence.

In this way, Upāli, the training of those bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna is deeply penetrated; it is a continuous training, whereas that of those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas is not.

Therefore, Upāli, you should speak of the training of those bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna as one that involves protection, entails exceptions, and is deeply entered; but you should speak of the training of those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle as one that is without protection, without exceptions, and accompanied by reproach. For what reason?

"Indeed, Upāli, supreme perfect enlightenment is of great accumulation; it is not easy for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna and is fixed in one-pointedness to sustain [the practice] and wander through cyclic existence for immeasurable and incalculable eons.
And seeing this purpose, Upāli, the Tathāgata, the perfectly enlightened one, [teaches] those who have not set out in the Mahāyāna..."
A bodhisattva does not speak exclusively of talk concerning world-weariness, nor does he speak exclusively of talk concerning dispassion, nor does he speak exclusively of talk concerning agitation;
rather, on the contrary, he speaks of talk concerning joy, talk concerning gladness, and talk associated with dependent origination.
He speaks a discourse that is profound, undefiled, subtle, and free from remorse; he speaks a discourse free from the outbursts of the afflictions;
he speaks a discourse on emptiness that is unattached and unobstructed.
Having heard this discourse, they become delighted, do not grow weary, and fulfill the accumulations for awakening.
Then, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, regarding these offenses—some are associated with attachment, some are associated with aversion, and some are associated with delusion."
"In that regard, Blessed One, what are the most serious transgressions of a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna?
Are they associated with attachment, or are they associated with aversion, or are they associated with delusion?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Upāli:

Upāli, if a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna were to commit offenses associated with passion as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and were to commit even a single offense associated with hatred— taking the Bodhisattvayāna as the standard— that offense associated with hatred is more grave than those others.
For what reason? Upāli, hatred leads to the abandonment of sentient beings, whereas attachment leads to the gathering of sentient beings.
In this regard, Upāli, concerning that affliction which leads to the gathering of sentient beings, the bodhisattva has neither deception nor fear;
concerning that affliction which leads to the abandonment of sentient beings, the bodhisattva has both deception and fear.
Moreover, Upāli, it was said previously: "Attachment is slow to fade away and is a minor transgression; hatred fades away quickly and is a major transgression.
In this regard, Upāli, that affliction which is slow to fade away and is a minor transgression is permissible for a bodhisattva;
however, that affliction which fades away quickly and is a major transgression is not at all appropriate for a bodhisattva, even in his dreams.
Therefore, Upāli, you should hold this in mind: whatever offenses of bodhisattvas are associated with passion (*rāga*), all of them are non-offenses.
In this regard, Upāli, those bodhisattvas who are unskilled in means (*anupāyakauśala*) fear offenses associated with passion, but not those associated with hatred (*dveṣa*).
However, those bodhisattvas who are skilled in means fear offenses associated with hatred, but not those associated with passion.
Then, indeed, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was present and seated in that very assembly.
Being seated, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, discipline is for the sake of awakening to all phenomena that are ultimately disciplined."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, if foolish ordinary people were to know all phenomena as being fundamentally disciplined, then the Tathāgata would no longer need to establish discipline."

Because sentient beings do not find delight [in the truth], the Tathāgata, based on fundamental reflection, prescribes the discipline for the realization of all phenomena that are utterly disciplined, in a gradual sequence.
Thus concludes the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa. 0.
